planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or set container plants in spring where roots can stay cool and moist but the stems can scramble up into afternoon shade; this is a canyon-bottom plant that resents hot, dry, fully exposed sites.

directions: Arizona honeysuckle is a twining, woody vine of mid-elevation canyons along the Mogollon Rim and mountain ranges of central Arizona and western New Mexico, scrambling over boulders and understory shrubs in the dappled light beneath canyon-bottom oaks, maples, and pines. Its slender, orange-red tubular flowers open through late spring and summer and are a strong draw for hummingbirds, followed by small translucent red berries favored by songbirds. Unlike the showier cultivated Asian honeysuckles, it is a modest, well-behaved native that stays loosely twining rather than smothering, making it suitable for training on a rustic trellis or allowing to ramble through a native shrub border. It is most at home with its roots in cool, humus-rich soil and its foliage reaching toward broken canopy light, reflecting its origin in narrow, shaded canyon drainages.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, rocky, well-drained soil beneath the broken canopy of oak-pine canyon woodland; Wright's silktassel establishes slowly and resents summer transplanting into open, unshaded ground.

directions: Wright's silktassel is an evergreen shrub of the rocky canyon slopes and oak-pine woodlands of the Sky Island ranges of southeastern Arizona, New Mexico, and the Trans-Pecos, typically rooted in the partial shade of taller canyon-slope trees rather than in open exposure. Its stiff, leathery, gray-green leaves and pendant, catkin-like flower clusters in spring give it a quietly textural presence through the year, and its small blue-black berries are an important food source for canyon-dwelling birds. Once established in its native rocky, well-drained substrate, it needs very little supplemental water and tolerates the intense heat and aridity of its native range as long as its roots are shaded from the hottest afternoon sun. It is a slow but durable choice for recreating the understory structure of a Southwest canyon woodland garden.

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions in spring into constantly moist, humus-rich soil at the base of a shaded seep, spring run, or stream terrace; this fern will not tolerate drying out and needs the deep, reliable shade of a canyon wall or riparian canopy.

directions: Sonoran maiden fern forms spreading colonies along perennial seeps and shaded stream terraces in the lower canyons of southern Arizona, such as those cutting through the Santa Catalina and Santa Rita mountains, where permanent water and canyon-wall shade create a pocket of humidity within the surrounding desert. Its broad, once-pinnate fronds arise from creeping rhizomes and give a lush, almost subtropical texture that contrasts sharply with the surrounding desert scrub. It needs the deep, constant shade and steady moisture of its native seep habitat to thrive and will scorch or decline quickly if exposed to direct sun or allowed to dry out. In a garden setting it is best reserved for the shaded margin of a water feature or a consistently irrigated courtyard bed in the warmer parts of its range.

planting.note: Wedge divisions into rock crevices or a sharply drained, gravelly substrate on a partially shaded canyon wall or rock garden face; established plants need little water and resent sitting in rich, moisture-retentive soil.

directions: Spiny cliffbrake is a small, drought-tolerant fern that roots directly into rock crevices on canyon walls and rocky slopes across Arizona, New Mexico, west Texas, and California, often tucked into the partial shade of a north-facing ledge or overhang rather than growing in open soil. Its stiff, blue-green fronds are made up of small, rounded leaflets tipped with a short bristle, giving the species its 'spiny' common name and a distinctive beaded texture among cliff-dwelling ferns. Unlike moisture-dependent maidenhair and shield ferns, it curls and appears to wither during extended drought, then rehydrates and greens up again within days of rain, a resilience adapted to its exposed canyon-wall habitat. It is a good choice for a lean, well-drained crevice or dry-stacked rock garden feature that recreates its native rocky microhabitat rather than a conventional moist shade bed.
